acceptance_criteria: AC-0 -- PURPOSE (read this first, it is the Product Owner's own explanation of why this matters, not background color): today's console (`py main.py --console`) is a thin wrapper reusing collection modules built for static HTML/JSON export -- it is not a real operational tool: it showed content on first load, then broke when a real job ran. The Product Owner's actual product goal is a genuinely usable, production-grade operator console -- the kind of tool a real network security team runs daily to onboard devices, pull configuration/inventory, run compliance checks, manage backups, and monitor failover readiness -- not a demo. UI 2.0 is that product's first real definition. It must be built right, even if that means a large, deliberate, incremental commitment (a new language stack, a new auth model, a real backup subsystem) rather than a quick patch on the existing static-export console. Every design choice in this movement should be evaluated against that bar: would a real operator trust and rely on this daily?

AC-1 (Purpose and parallel-track model): document explicitly, as its own section, the Product Owner's operating model decided this morning: two tracks run in parallel and do not block each other. Track A ('Line-1') is the existing Python feature/collection-module development (M-series, PCC, etc.) -- it continues exactly as before, indefinitely. Track B is UI 2.0 itself. As a Track-A feature matures (reaches real-environment validation), it is ported/evolved into UI 2.0 one feature at a time -- never a stop-the-world migration of everything at once. This design must describe HOW that per-feature migration actually works mechanically (what changes about a feature when it moves from 'a Python collection module feeding a static export' to 'a UI 2.0-integrated Java service'), not just state the principle.

AC-2 (C-1, resolved -- amend CON.0): UI 2.0 is a separate shell/application from today's console, NOT built inside the existing console's payload model. This requires amending CON.0 section 6 from 'the console never introduces a payload shape the exporter does not also produce' to 'both surfaces read the same persisted projections' (both UI 2.0 and the static exporter read from the same underlying database/projection layer, they no longer need to produce byte-identical payload shapes), and narrowing CON.0 section 3's bundler rule to apply only to the shared report bundle, not to UI 2.0 itself. Document the exact proposed replacement wording for both frozen sections, in the same style AC-CS's own frozen sections are written, ready for a Product Owner freeze decision -- do not just describe the change, draft the actual amended text.

AC-3 (C-2, resolved -- RBAC is D1/D7, never menu-hiding): role-based screen/menu authorization is NOT implemented as hiding menu entries by role. It is implemented exactly as the frozen AC-CS-33 already requires: every navigation entry always renders per D1 (surface eligibility), every action shows its own D7 (authorization) outcome, and the server refuses an unauthorized action -- the UI communicates 'you cannot do this and here is why' rather than making the option disappear. Design the concrete role model on top of this: an operator's AD-group membership (per M14's LDAP design) maps to a set of D7-authorized actions; design how that mapping is expressed, stored, and evaluated per-request in UI 2.0's own request path (server-side, never a client-side visibility toggle).

AC-4 (C-3, resolved -- Backbox-style profile-based backup subsystem, browser UI): design UI 2.0's backup subsystem in real detail, modeled explicitly on Backbox's own approach (the Product Owner will share reference screenshots separately -- design generously and note where a screenshot would resolve an open UI detail, don't block on it): (a) device addition/onboarding is code-driven -- reuses the existing Device Registry (PCP.1) and discovery/manual enrollment, NOT part of the backup subsystem itself; (b) backup is profile-based -- a profile (e.g. 'CP R81.20') is an ordered sequence of steps, each step being an SSH/SFTP interaction with an expected-response validation gate (connect -> expect a prompt/banner -> proceed; each step's success is checked before the next runs, exactly like an expect script) -- this must work even for a device/vendor the product has no native collector for, as long as SSH/SFTP is reachable and the operator manually authors the step sequence per that vendor's own admin guide; (c) there is no single static built-in backup method -- backup is entirely profile-driven and operator-configurable; (d) the UI itself shows backup state/readiness/history and lets an operator create/select a profile, select target devices, and set a schedule -- reconcile this explicitly against utils/action_taxonomy.py's class 1 submission boundary and the C-D7 gate (per the requirements draft's own C-3 analysis): design exactly which parts of this flow are a browser-safe read/schedule-intent action versus which parts require a CLI/file-level operation, and what D7-authorized, audited schedule-edit intent looks like if the browser needs to trigger one.

AC-5 (C-4, resolved -- concurrent multi-admin, single-session-per-user): UI 2.0's authentication must support multiple administrators working concurrently (e.g. 3 admins simultaneously, each with their own live session), but a single admin identity must not be logged in from more than one active session/screen at a time (logging in elsewhere should end or refuse the prior session, operator's choice which). Design this as the successor to DEPLOY.1A's auth shape, using LDAP (per M14's design) instead of OIDC, reusing M14's A1/A2 split and LD-1/LD-2/LD-3/LD-4/LD-6 decisions where they still apply to a multi-user server context rather than M14's own single-operator TTY-bind scope -- name explicitly which M14 decisions carry over unchanged and which need a multi-user-specific amendment (e.g. LD-3's in-memory-only state doesn't survive a multi-process/multi-user server the same way).

AC-6 (U-1, resolved -- full Java stack, incremental per-feature port): UI 2.0's entire stack (service layer, API, DB access, and every feature once it's migrated) is Java, not just a thin new layer over Python workers. Design the migration mechanics per AC-1's model: for one concrete example feature (pick the CE.2 compliance-check-primitives work merged last night as the worked example, since it is real and recent), describe concretely what porting it to Java looks like -- the primitive registry's shape in Java, how the read-only safety boundary is enforced in the new language, what test-parity proof is required before the Python version is retired for that feature. State the language/library choices this implies (a JVM web framework, a DB access layer, a build/packaging approach) with tradeoffs, matching the rigor M14's own LD-5 (library choice) decision used.

AC-7 (X-2, already resolved -- record, don't re-derive): PostgreSQL is the frozen production storage engine for UI 2.0's control-plane/projection/audit state; SQLite remains the local engine unchanged; content-addressed evidence blobs and the recovery store stay on the filesystem volume unchanged. Oracle was considered (corporate default) and explicitly deferred, not rejected -- record that a future corporate mandate could still introduce it, and that today's storage-access design should not make an Oracle option needlessly hard, without spending further design effort on it now.

AC-8: produce docs/design/UI2_0_ARCHITECTURE_DESIGN.md capturing AC-0 through AC-7 as a coherent, freeze-ready document (status DRAFT) -- ready for the Product Owner to share externally for a second opinion and eventually run through a formal decision process, not yet authorizing implementation.
AC-9: update project/backlog.json's relevant note(s) (ui2_0_architecture_requirements and/or a new entry for this design) pointing at the new document and its resolved-vs-still-open status.

AC-10: no implementation, no test changes, no code changes beyond the new document and the backlog note -- same validation floor as prior design-only movements (git diff --check, privacy gate, no code/test touched).
